newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Gov. denies backing down on his welfare plan.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Gov. denies backing down on his welfare plan.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki denied Thursday he had retreated from a plan to cut welfare benefits according to a sliding scale, saying a New York Times report that he had done so was not correct.

"Nothing is off the table. The Times article that we abandoned certain positions is completely inaccurate. I never said that yesterday and I've never said that in private leaders' meetings," Pataki told reporters in Albany. He was referring to the negotiations he has been holding with the Senate Majority Leader and the Assembly Speaker.

The Times, in its Thursday edition, said Pataki indicated that he was willing to back away from key elements of his plan, including a proposal to gradually reduce cash benefits to poor families by 45 percent over five years.

The battle over the state's welfare plan has prevented lawmakers from aggreeing on a new budget for fiscal 1997, which was due on April 1. Should the state fail to get a new pact before July 13, it risks setting a new, national record for tardy budgets for the second year in a row.

The Republican Governor's welfare plan calls for level benefits in the first 18 months, followed by a 10 percent cut in the first year, another five percent in the second, and 15 percent each year after that. The Democrat-led Assembly has fought the scheme, as has the Republican-led Senate.

When asked if he and the Assembly Speaker opposed the governor's plan for benefit reductions, State Senate Majority Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, said: "We are in different places, all three of us right now in the cuts.

"We have had a proposal up there that cuts in a different way the benefits. Ten percent is my recollection over several years, with the recognition that the federal government has mandated that in five years people are off welfare in this state, other than the minimum number, and those would fall into a safety net."

Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, who reiterated his objections to reducing benefits, said he did not know if the governor had dropped his proposed cuts. "I don't know if it's off the table, the governor is sitting obviously with his position on it, but I have indicated to you that I don't think we are in any way going to be doing harsh and inhumane cuts."

Silver appeared a bit more optimistic than Pataki that the negotiations would reach the final stages over the weekend. Another leaders' meeting was expected later this evening, while staffers will be back at work on Saturday. "We anticipate that by Sunday night or Monday morning we will be in a position to accumulate all of that and perhaps go forward with the concluding process."
However, Pataki said only that that scenario was possible, adding he did not want to raise expectations.
